title: Four Things I Wish Someone Had Told Me When I Was a Student Teacher
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart distills a twenty-minute keynote to 400 West Michigan student teachers into four things he wishes he had known: teaching is hard, noble, malleable, and worth it. He opens with his own cautionary story, beginning as an aspiring movie-hero teacher and burning out within three years in Baltimore. The central move is to replace the savior-technician self-image with a professional's expectation of difficulty, while anchoring the work's meaning in service rather than in policy or public respect. He ties malleability to the internal work of cultivating key beliefs, so that even hard assignments can make a teacher better. The piece closes with a long-career vision in which small yearly improvements compound into large effects on students' lives.
points: Stuart's early self-image as a savior-technician, always one strategy from greatness, left him unprepared for the ordinary difficulty of a profession.
He argues teaching's nobility as service is untouched by policy, culture shifts, or relatives' opinions, even though those factors change its circumstances.
Teachers' experience of the work is malleable: cultivating the right internal beliefs lets even the hardest assignment improve a teacher's craft.
He frames longevity as the payoff, imagining what ten to thirty years of getting five percent better each year would do for students.
Stuart opens with his own burnout and year away from the classroom to give the advice credibility with novices.
quotes: In my head early on, I was always just one strategy or technique away from greatness. I wouldn't have verbalized this, but I functionally viewed teaching as a savior-technician's job, not a professional's.

When you don't expect teaching to be riddled with challenge, you're like a five-year-old doing a puzzle on the living room floor who doesn't expect her toddler sister to come rampaging through any moment.

But the thing is, teaching is inherently noble — its nobility can't be touched by policies or culture-shifts or politics or parents. The circumstances of teaching can surely be changed by these factors, but at the end of the day, teachers still seek to give something to their students that they will carry with them for life.
If we cultivate the key beliefs in ourselves, then even the hardest teaching assignments can work toward our good, toward us getting better at the internal and external work of teaching.
How many lives would they impact if, for each of those years, they became five percent better? It's beyond quantification.

The full and engaged teaching career is one of the most powerful forces on the planet. I'm convinced of that. If only we had eyes to see the gargantuan ripples emanating from the life of the joyfully engaged teacher.
